query: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Premelting and melting in high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles are governed by the preferential surface segregation of lower surface energy elements, which forms a liquid‐like, disordered layer that locally reduces the melting point well below the bulk value.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic or near‐equiatomic HEA nanoparticles (sub‐10 nm) prepared as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution on an inert substrate.
generation.intervention: In situ TEM heating of the HEA nanoparticles with sequential STEM imaging and compositional (EDS) mapping while ramping temperature from room temperature to near the bulk melting point.
generation.conditions: High vacuum with controlled temperature steps (e.g., 300 K up to 1200 K) and uniform nanoparticle size/composition; additional controlled studies with post‐synthesis surface modifications to alter effective surface energy.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a surface layer enriched in lower surface energy elements that becomes disordered and liquid‐like prior to complete melting.
generation.mechanism: Thermodynamic differences in elemental surface energies drive faster diffusion of the lower surface energy metal(s) to the nanoparticle surface. This leads to the formation of a localized, disordered layer with a lower melting point than the well‐mixed interior. The existence of this surface layer promotes premelting behavior before the remainder of the nanoparticle reaches the bulk melting temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: In situ characterization will reveal the onset of surface disorder (evidenced by STEM imaging and EDS showing elemental enrichment) at temperatures significantly lower than the bulk melting point. Nanoparticles with modified surface energies (by ligand exchange or other treatments) will exhibit a delayed premelting onset relative to untreated particles.
generation.baseline: If high entropy stabilization prevailed uniformly without surface segregation, the nanoparticles would remain uniformly crystalline up to the predicted bulk melting point, with no early surface premelting.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected for sub‐10 nm HEA nanoparticles with a narrow size distribution and equiatomic compositions. The mechanism may differ for larger nanoparticles or systems with preexisting compositional inhomogeneities.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature range for the onset of surface segregation and the quantitative impact of the nanoparticle shape and size on the melting characteristics remain uncertain and may vary across compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ TEM studies combining high-resolution imaging with STEM-EDS mapping during controlled heating. Compare untreated HEA nanoparticles with those subjected to a surface-modifying treatment designed to suppress segregation. Monitor the temperature at which a disordered, compositionally segregated surface layer appears and document the corresponding morphological changes.
measurements: Temperature-dependent STEM-EDS profiles for surface vs. core elemental composition
High-resolution TEM imaging to detect onset and progression of surface disorder
Comparison of onset temperatures of premelting behavior between modified and unmodified nanoparticles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no measurable surface segregation or formation of a disordered liquid-like layer is detected prior to bulk melting, or if surface treatments do not alter the onset temperature of premelting relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is rejected.
